cells.tense: You're at the door with steady hands for what's arriving.
cells.ask: Let one thing you're looking after come to its own shape today, hands off — then notice what that frees in you.
cells.core:
What's coming in gets met by you, and it grows because you don't crowd it. You keep the conditions right, you pay attention, and then you let the thing be what it is. People feel that room even when they can't name it, and they stay because of it — not because you handed them the answer, but because you didn't need to.

So when something you've been carrying reaches its own full shape, stepping back isn't a loss. You put the hours in, and then you let it stand on its own. That release is completion, not the price of it.
cells.sheetLine: You're tending what's arriving without forcing it, and that steadiness is holding.
cells.verb: tending what's forming, keeping conditions right without forcing the pace
cells.place: at the door where what's coming in gets met, before it's been sorted

cells.tense: You're already several moves into what hasn't arrived yet.
cells.ask: Name one thing you're holding on someone else's behalf, and set it down for today — no announcement, hands off.
cells.core:
Care in good conditions looks like open hands: you meet what's arriving, you keep it warm, and you let it take its own time. Braced ahead of the arrival, the hands close. You start steering what should be growing on its own — deciding its shape before it has shown you one, and calling that care.

That hold feels like love from the inside, and it wears both of you out. You don't have to see the whole way ahead. Keeping the door open instead of walking through it for someone else is enough, and it's what today is asking of you.

cells.tense: You're standing at a door that closed a while back, still waiting for a knock.
cells.ask: Pick one living thing to tend today — a plant, a page, a person who'd notice — and give it five minutes without finishing it.
cells.core:
In good conditions this is a person at the door meeting whatever shows up, care going out, things growing on their own, you in the middle of it. What's here instead is a shut door and a story that you're fine by yourself. Nothing new is getting in because nothing is being invited.

Something still wants to grow, and it's got nowhere to put it. Start smaller than feels worth doing — one thing kept alive for a few days, without asking it to mean anything yet. The pull toward what you actually want doesn't need to be aimed. It just needs somewhere to point.
cells.sheetLine: The caring part of you has gone quiet, and nothing new can get in while it's shut.

cells.tense: You're carrying a role you never agreed to, and carrying it well enough that no one has said anything.
cells.ask: Find one thing in your week that's someone else's to hold, and stop doing it — no explanation, just stop.
cells.core:
People come to you and you hold them, and that much is really happening. From the outside it probably looks like a gift — steady, warm, dependable. What hasn't happened is you deciding it was yours to do. The care runs on its own, and you keep feeding it while you feel scraped thin.

You don't have to keep carrying it to stay the person who cares. Letting one thing go isn't abandoning anyone — it gives the care a shape you actually chose. What gets set down gets set down because it wasn't yours to begin with, not because you failed at holding it.
cells.sheetLine: You're already tending what's at the door, and you still haven't said it's your choice to.

attempts.check: The record supports a shift in stance toward Nurturing in the Source seat — the seat where what's arriving gets met. It doesn't support a claim about what's actually arriving for this person: whether it's a person, a project, a diagnosis, a child. So the cells describe the posture, never the content of the arrival. A reader could reasonably say 'I'm not a caretaker' or 'I don't control anyone' — the Too Much and Too Little cells name a behaviour pattern, and if it doesn't fit, the ask still stands as an experiment on its own. The ask in each cell survives a wrong read because it's a small, observable act, not contingent on my being right about them. The sentence that risks serving me more than the reader is the sheetLine on Too Much — 'the armour' is mine, not theirs, and it's doing the work of a metaphor the cell doesn't need.
